What the Ladder of Inference Does to Your Supply Chain Decisions

The story we tell ourselves about a difficult interaction can move faster than the evidence.

Pupsi Phull · Phull Insights22 September 20262 min readLeadership & Transformation
Evidence boundary

Personal analysis and professional reflection based on earlier postgraduate work. Named-company examples describe historical research, not current 2026 corporate policies, figures or commitments. No unpublished case result is represented as a verified outcome.

Why this matters

A missed commitment or tense meeting quickly invites a conclusion about motive. That conclusion can then shape every subsequent conversation.

What the evidence suggests

The Ladder of Inference is a useful way to slow this movement from observation to belief. It asks which facts were noticed, what meaning was added, and where an assumption began to look like certainty.

What it looks like in practice

In a supplier dispute, write down the observable event before interpreting intent. Ask what alternative explanation could fit the same facts, then test it directly with the other party.

Practical next steps

Three things leaders can do now

01

Describe the event without adjectives or attributed motives.

02

Identify the first assumption that changed the meaning of the evidence.

03

Ask a question that could disconfirm your preferred explanation.

Phull Insights Perspective

The view beneath the headline.

Reflection is not indecision. It is a way to make difficult conversations more precise and more likely to produce a workable answer.
